paragraphs: Bayesian inverse problems seek an underlying signal that could explain an observation while accounting for uncertainty. A pretrained diffusion model can provide prior knowledge about plausible signals, allowing different reconstruction problems to be tackled at inference time without retraining a separate model for each task.

The difficulty is combining that prior with the observation throughout the diffusion sampling process. The intermediate distributions needed for posterior sampling have likelihood terms that cannot be evaluated tractably. The paper proposes approximating these distributions with mixtures. However, this alone does not make ordinary gradient-based sampling feasible: some required terms remain intractable. The authors therefore develop a practical sampling method based on Gibbs sampling.

The approach is evaluated on image inverse problems using diffusion priors operating both directly on pixels and in latent spaces, and on audio source separation. These experiments support the framework across different signal types and representations. Its central contribution is a mixture approximation paired with a sampling procedure that makes that approximation usable.
icml-2025-a-mixture-based-framework-for-.tldr: A mixture approximation and Gibbs-based sampling method use pretrained diffusion models to solve inverse problems without task-specific retraining.

paragraphs: Quantizing a language model reduces the precision used to store and compute its weights and activations. Fine-grained scaling helps accommodate unusually large values, but blocks of values can still have different distributions that a single number format represents poorly. BlockDialect addresses this mismatch by changing the available representations for each block.

The method selects a number format from a collection called a formatbook. Its DialectFP4 formatbook contains variants of four-bit floating-point representations designed for different distributions. A two-stage procedure handles activation quantization during execution. The representable values are scaled integers, allowing the method to use low-precision integer arithmetic and support energy-efficient computation.

Compared with MXFP4, the paper reports accuracy gains of 10.78% on LLaMA3-8B and 7.48% on LLaMA2-7B while using fewer bits per datum. The corresponding gaps below full precision are 5.45% and 2.69%, including full-path matrix multiplication quantization. These findings support adapting the number format itself as an additional way to preserve accuracy under aggressive quantization.
icml-2025-blockdialect-block-wise-fine-g.tldr: BlockDialect adapts four-bit number formats to individual data blocks, improving reported language-model accuracy while supporting efficient integer arithmetic.

paragraphs: Neural-network expressiveness is often studied as though computers could store arbitrary real numbers and perform exact arithmetic. Actual networks use floating-point numbers, so rounding and overflow can change what they compute. This paper asks which functions networks can represent when those computational realities are included in the mathematical model.

The key property is whether the first layer can distinguish its inputs. If two different inputs become the same representation there, later layers cannot assign them different outputs when needed. The authors establish this distinguishability as necessary for representing every function on the input domain. Under mild conditions on the activation function, they also prove that it is sufficient.

The resulting guarantees cover broad, activation-dependent domains and outputs that may be finite or infinite floating-point values. Sigmoid and tanh support all finite floating-point inputs. For ReLU and several other listed activations, the guarantee covers finite inputs whose magnitudes are less than one eighth of the largest float. The result establishes representational capacity under actual floating-point operations.
icml-2025-floating-point-neural-networks.tldr: Floating-point networks can represent every floating-point function on broad domains when their first layer distinguishes inputs and their activations satisfy mild conditions.

paragraphs: Many language-model weight matrices can be represented with lower-rank structure, potentially reducing storage and computation. This paper investigates why that structure emerges unevenly across a model. It studies how the subspaces occupied by gradients stabilize during training, using Hessian analysis to provide a theoretical account of that stabilization.

The authors empirically connect gradient dynamics with the extent to which weight matrices admit low-rank representations. Different components develop different degrees of low-rank structure, motivating compression that assigns different ranks to different matrices. Their method, Weight Low-Rank Projection, or WeLore, combines compression and memory-efficient fine-tuning through a data-agnostic, one-shot procedure.

WeLore separates matrices into components that are more or less amenable to low-rank representation. The reported findings suggest that the low-rank components also tend to be better candidates for fine-tuning. Updating only those components can closely follow, and sometimes outperform, full fine-tuning in training-loss trajectory and performance while reducing memory and computation. This connects compression choices with decisions about where adaptation should occur.
icml-2025-from-low-rank-gradient-subspac.tldr: WeLore uses uneven low-rank structure across language-model weights to combine compression with selective, resource-efficient fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Transfer learning aims to apply what a model has learned to new tasks, ideally without retraining. This paper makes the notion of a new task more precise through geometry in a Hilbert space. That perspective distinguishes different ways a target task can relate to the tasks available during learning.

The authors define three transfer regimes. Interpolation stays within the convex hull of known tasks, corresponding to weighted combinations with nonnegative weights that sum to one. A second regime allows extrapolation within their linear span, while a third reaches outside that span. They propose a function-encoder method intended to handle all three and introduce a training scheme based on least-squares optimization.

The paper also proves a universal approximation theorem for function encoders and compares the method with approaches including transformers and meta-learning. Across four benchmarks, it reports better performance than state-of-the-art methods in all three transfer regimes. The geometric distinction helps interpret these findings by identifying how the new tasks differ from the training tasks.
icml-2025-function-encoders-a-principled.tldr: Function encoders combine a geometric account of task transfer with least-squares training, outperforming compared methods across three transfer regimes on four benchmarks.

paragraphs: A Gaussian-process bandit algorithm must choose evaluations of an unknown reward function while limiting the reward lost through imperfect choices. This paper assumes that the function belongs to a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, which supplies the mathematical structure used to analyze learning and regret.

The main technical contribution is a sharper upper bound on the largest posterior variance, a measure of remaining uncertainty. The new bound improves how observation-noise variance enters the analysis. Using it, the authors refine maximum variance reduction and phased elimination algorithms. They obtain a nearly optimal regret bound without observation noise and bounds with optimal dependence on the reward function's RKHS norm.

The same analysis also covers observation noise whose variance changes over time. For that setting, the authors establish noise-dependent regret upper bounds for algorithms based on the two approaches, together with a matching lower bound. The contribution therefore concerns sharper performance guarantees across several noise regimes, with optimality stated for the particular settings and dependencies analyzed.
icml-2025-improved-regret-analysis-in-ga.tldr: A sharper posterior-variance bound yields improved Gaussian-process bandit regret guarantees for noiseless observations, RKHS norm dependence, and time-varying noise.

paragraphs: Consistency models aim to produce in one neural-network pass what score-based diffusion models generate through multiple sampling steps. This paper examines a difference between two ways of learning these models and proposes a new flow to improve consistency training.

Consistency distillation uses a pretrained network to approximate the velocity field of a differential equation: the directions that guide samples along their paths. Consistency training instead estimates that field using a single Monte Carlo sample. The authors show that the resulting estimation error creates a discrepancy between the two learning approaches. That discrepancy persists even in the continuous-time limit, so moving to that limit does not eliminate it.

The proposed flow moves noisy data toward their corresponding outputs from a consistency model. This lets the model’s outputs help define the transport process used to address the estimation problem. The authors prove that the flow reduces both the identified discrepancy and the cost of transporting noise toward data.

The paper reports faster convergence and improved overall performance for consistency training. Its contribution connects an explanation of why the two learning approaches differ with a change to the transport flow that reduces that difference.
icml-2025-improving-consistency-models-w.tldr: A flow guided by consistency-model outputs reduces a discrepancy between consistency training and distillation, accelerating training convergence and improving performance.

paragraphs: Randomized experiments rely on participants sharing outcomes that may be sensitive. Differential privacy provides formal privacy guarantees, but mechanisms that add noise can make estimated causal effects less precise. This paper studies how to reduce that variance penalty while preserving the privacy protection.

The proposed mechanism, Cluster-DP, uses a supplied clustering of the data. The authors develop results that apply to any clustering and introduce a quality metric for judging which cluster structures are more helpful. Their analysis shows that choosing higher-quality clusters according to this metric can reduce the additional variance caused by privacy without weakening the privacy guarantees.

The paper evaluates Cluster-DP theoretically and empirically using real and simulated data. Comparisons include common baselines and two versions that are special cases of the same framework: an unclustered version and a uniform-prior version. This makes clustering a concrete design choice in private causal estimation and connects the usefulness of that choice to an explicit measure of cluster quality.
icml-2025-improving-the-variance-of-diff.tldr: Cluster-DP uses data clusters to reduce the variance cost of private causal estimation, with better clusters offering improvements without weaker privacy guarantees.

paragraphs: In formal reasoning, symbols can need distinct identities without having distinct semantic roles. Renaming a bound variable can preserve an expression's meaning, a property called alpha-equivalence. The paper argues that language models lack a suitable notion of such interchangeable tokens, making unfamiliar symbols and expanding vocabularies difficult to handle.

The authors formalize this problem and introduce alpha-covariance as a metric for robustness to these transformations. Their embedding design gives each token two components. A shared component represents semantic consistency across interchangeable symbols, while a randomized component keeps individual tokens distinguishable. The design therefore preserves both the common role and the identity information that reasoning tasks require.

Compared with a baseline trained using alpha-renaming as data augmentation, the method generalizes better to unseen tokens in linear temporal logic solving, propositional logic assignment prediction, and copying with an expandable vocabulary. The results support an architectural inductive bias toward alpha-equivalence and show how embedding design can help models handle new symbols systematically.
icml-2025-interchangeable-token-embeddin.tldr: Shared and randomized embedding components help models treat symbols as semantically interchangeable while preserving identity and generalizing to unseen tokens.

paragraphs: Large linear programs can be costly to solve because they contain many variables. This paper trains a neural network to generate a projection matrix tailored to each problem instance. The projection reduces the number of variables, creating a smaller optimization problem from which feasible solutions can be obtained.

Training uses multiple linear programs and maximizes expected objective value, encouraging projections that retain useful solution quality. The architecture incorporates permutation equivariance and invariance so it can handle differently sized problems and their variable or constraint orderings. Because the projection changes the problem presented to a solver, the approach is solver-agnostic and can shorten computation for different linear-programming solvers.

The authors also provide a generalization-bound analysis for learning these projection matrices. In experiments, the method produces higher-quality solutions than existing reduction methods and takes substantially less time than solving the original programs. The contribution is a learned way to choose a smaller search space while retaining feasibility and useful objective values for newly encountered problems.
icml-2025-learning-to-generate-projectio.tldr: A neural network learns instance-specific projections that reduce linear-program size and enable faster, high-quality feasible solutions across heterogeneous problems.

paragraphs: Independently trained networks can use different parameter orderings while representing comparable solutions. Permuting their parameters can reveal low-loss linear connections that were previously hidden. This paper asks whether methods that align two networks also place several networks together in an approximately convex region of low test loss.

The empirical analysis finds that existing pairwise permutation-search methods can fail at this multi-model task. The authors introduce STE-MM, which searches for permutations across multiple models using a straight-through estimator. In their experiments, merging models aligned this way produces test loss close to that of the original models, while loss barriers between every aligned pair remain small.

The authors additionally examine local loss sharpness through the trace of the Hessian matrix. With STE-MM, sharpness around the merged model decreases as more models are included. These observations provide empirical support for multi-model linear connectivity after suitable alignment. They also show why successful alignment of an individual pair does not automatically establish compatible alignment for an entire collection.
icml-2025-linear-mode-connectivity-betwe.tldr: STE-MM jointly aligns multiple networks through parameter permutations, empirically enabling low-loss merging and small barriers between aligned model pairs.

paragraphs: Training procedures have an implicit bias: they favor some solutions over others even when several solutions fit the data. Explicit regularization, such as weight decay, also influences learning. This paper studies how these two influences interact, focusing on how regularization can change the bias produced by the training dynamics.

The authors incorporate explicit regularization into the mirror-flow framework, a geometric description of optimization dynamics. Their analysis identifies three lasting effects: positional bias, changes in the type of bias, and range shrinking. The framework covers problems including sparse coding, matrix sensing, single-layer attention, and LoRA, giving the analysis relevance across several forms of model training.

A practical implication is that regularization can continue to matter after it is removed because it has already shaped the training trajectory. The authors propose switching weight decay off during training and demonstrate experimentally that doing so can improve generalization. This supports considering dynamic weight-decay schedules, with the benefit framed as a possibility demonstrated in experiments rather than a universal outcome.
icml-2025-mirror-mirror-of-the-flow-how-.tldr: A mirror-flow analysis shows how regularization can durably reshape implicit bias and motivates switching off weight decay during training.

paragraphs: Code generation can involve repeated attempts, with execution feedback helping a model revise earlier solutions. Training for this interaction can become complicated when rewards must account for an entire sequence of revisions. This paper proposes μCODE, which learns to use multi-turn feedback while relying only on single-step rewards.

The approach rests on viewing code generation as a one-step recoverable decision process: from any intermediate code state, a correct program can be produced in one turn. This makes immediate candidate quality useful even within a longer interaction. μCODE iteratively trains a generator conditioned on the accumulated execution feedback and a verifier that scores newly produced code.

The experiments report significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines and show that the method uses execution feedback effectively. The paper also analyzes choices concerning the reward models and generation policy. Its main contribution is a simpler training approach for iterative code generation, grounded in the ability to replace an unsuccessful program with a correct solution in a single revision.
icml-2025-multi-turn-code-generation-thr.tldr: μCODE trains a feedback-conditioned code generator and verifier with single-step rewards to improve multi-turn code generation.

paragraphs: Completing a matrix becomes especially difficult when entire rows and columns are missing. In the setting studied here, the target matrix cannot be estimated without additional information. Motivated by biological problems, the paper uses a related source matrix that is itself noisy and incomplete, with the relationship described by a feature shift in latent space.

The authors study both passive sampling and active sampling, where the method can choose which target rows and columns to query. They establish minimax lower bounds on entrywise estimation error in each setting. These bounds characterize the best achievable worst-case accuracy under the respective sampling conditions.

Their computationally efficient framework reaches the lower bound in the active setting by using source information to select informative target queries. This avoids the incoherence assumptions needed for rate optimality under passive sampling. Comparisons on real biological datasets demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The result connects useful transfer to both the source-target relationship and the ability to choose what target information to collect.
icml-2025-optimal-transfer-learning-for-.tldr: Source-guided active sampling enables an efficient matrix-completion method to attain optimal entrywise error bounds when entire target rows and columns are missing.

paragraphs: Multi-objective Bayesian optimization searches for good tradeoffs between competing objectives. One strategy chooses evaluations based on how much they are expected to reveal about the Pareto frontier, the set of tradeoffs that cannot be improved in one objective without worsening another. Computing this information gain requires a predictive distribution conditioned on that frontier.

The conditioning truncates the predictive distribution, but the complete frontier is usually unavailable in a continuous domain. The paper approximates the required distribution using a mixture of two truncations that can be constructed from a partial frontier. These over- and under-truncations provide different approximations, and their best relative weighting is not known beforehand.

The authors learn the mixture balance by maximizing a variational lower bound, providing a way to minimize approximation error in the information-gain calculation. Empirical evaluation supports the method's effectiveness, particularly with many objectives. The contribution is therefore a tractable way to improve the information used for choosing evaluations when only part of the frontier is available.
icml-2025-pareto-frontier-entropy-search.tldr: An optimized mixture of approximate truncations improves Pareto-frontier information-gain estimation, especially in optimization problems with many objectives.

paragraphs: Federated ensemble distillation combines predictions from client models to label an unlabeled server dataset, then trains a server model on those pseudo-labels. When clients have very different data, the weights assigned to their predictions become especially important. A weighting rule determines how strongly each client influences the resulting training targets.

The paper proposes a weighting method inspired by theoretical results from generative adversarial networks. Clients train discriminators using their local datasets and a generator distributed by the server. Those discriminators supply the information used to weight client predictions. The authors provide a near-optimality guarantee for the proposed weighting approach.

Image-classification experiments show significant improvements over the compared baselines. The paper also reports negligible additional communication cost, client computation, and client-side privacy leakage. It considers both a pre-existing unlabeled server dataset and a data-free route for generating one. The contribution is a theoretically supported way to account for client heterogeneity while keeping the added operational burden small in the evaluated settings.
icml-2025-provably-near-optimal-federate.tldr: Client-trained discriminators provide a provably near-optimal weighting rule for federated distillation, improving reported accuracy with negligible added overhead.

paragraphs: Serving several fine-tuned mixture-of-experts language models on one GPU is difficult because their combined weights demand substantial memory. Conventional resource partitioning can limit how effectively that GPU serves the models together. This paper proposes sharing similar expert components across models to reduce their total memory footprint.

Sharing experts is paired with runtime partial reconfiguration: the system dynamically replaces non-expert layers when requests switch between models. This preserves model-specific processing while allowing consolidated experts to remain shared. The reported system maintains competitive output quality and throughput comparable to serving a single model, with only a negligible increase in time to the first generated token.

On an 80GB NVIDIA A100 using Mixtral-8x7B models, experiments show an average 85% reduction in turnaround time relative to NVIDIA's multi-instance GPU approach. Tests with up to four Switch Transformer Base-8 variants also support scalability and output-quality preservation compared with model-merging baselines. The results demonstrate how selective sharing and request-dependent reconfiguration can make multi-model serving more efficient.
icml-2025-qos-efficient-serving-of-multi.tldr: Sharing similar experts and swapping non-expert layers at runtime enables efficient serving of multiple fine-tuned MoE models on one GPU.

paragraphs: Domain generalization asks a model to work beyond the domains represented in its training data. Overfitting to those source domains is a central obstacle. QT-DoG uses quantization-aware training to address that obstacle, treating reduced weight precision as a source of regularization as well as a way to shrink models.

The proposed explanation is that quantization introduces noise into model weights and steers optimization toward flatter minima. In such regions, small weight perturbations have less effect on the loss. The paper provides an analytical perspective and empirical evidence linking weight quantization to this flatter geometry and to improved generalization across domains.

The authors also use the smaller size of quantized models to build an ensemble. They report that combining multiple quantized models surpasses state-of-the-art domain-generalization approaches without additional computational or memory overhead in their comparison. The findings give quantization two connected roles: shaping the training dynamics of individual models and making it possible to combine several compact models within the reported resource budget.
icml-2025-qt-dog-quantization-aware-trai.tldr: QT-DoG uses weight quantization as regularization to encourage flatter minima and improve domain generalization, including through compact-model ensembles.

paragraphs: Many optimization problems add together costs contributed by individual data points. A robust version can discard the largest m costs, reducing the influence of outliers. This paper develops a general way to compress such robust objectives into weighted subsets, called coresets, while preserving an approximation guarantee.

The construction starts from properties of the original, untrimmed problem. If its total sensitivity is T and it admits a standard coreset of size S, the robust coreset has size roughly mT divided by the approximation tolerance, plus S, with logarithmic factors suppressed. This explicitly relates the extra compression cost of robustness to the number of discarded contributions and the sensitivity of the original objective.

For Euclidean subspace embedding, the authors show that the coreset size is near-tight. They also report scalable running time and new or improved algorithms for robust optimization problems. On real datasets, the resulting coresets outperform uniform sampling. The framework makes robust compression depend on reusable properties of the underlying non-robust problem.
icml-2025-robust-sparsification-via-sens.tldr: A sensitivity-based framework constructs compact weighted approximations for objectives that discard outliers, with near-tight size guarantees for Euclidean subspace embedding.

paragraphs: Federated learning can spend substantial communication on high-dimensional model updates. Compressors such as Top-K reduce what is transmitted, but compression can damage optimization performance. Error feedback addresses this problem, yet much of its existing theory concerns smooth objectives without constraints. The paper extends the analysis to non-smooth convex optimization with safety constraints.

The authors first establish lower complexity bounds for first-order algorithms that use contractive compression. These bounds set a theoretical benchmark for the resources such algorithms require. They then introduce Safe-EF, which matches their lower bound up to a constant while enforcing safety constraints. An extension covers stochastic optimization, bringing the method closer to settings with uncertain update information.

Experiments use a reinforcement-learning setup simulating distributed training of humanoid robots. The reported results support both safety enforcement and reduced communication complexity. The paper's contribution combines a lower-bound analysis with an algorithm designed to attain it, expanding error feedback to a setting where non-smoothness and constraints are central parts of the optimization problem.
icml-2025-safe-ef-error-feedback-for-non.tldr: Safe-EF extends error feedback to non-smooth constrained optimization, matching a compression-related lower bound up to a constant while enforcing safety constraints.

paragraphs: One-step generative models aim to produce samples with a single generation step. Score-of-Mixture Training, or SMT, provides a framework for learning these models by reducing a particular discrepancy between real and generated data: the alpha-skew Jensen–Shannon divergence. Its central learning signal comes from mixtures of the two kinds of samples.

SMT estimates the score of those mixture distributions at multiple noise levels. A score describes how a distribution's log density changes with the input, providing information about its local structure. The framework supports training a generator from scratch. It also supports transferring knowledge from a pretrained diffusion model through a variant called Score-of-Mixture Distillation, or SMD.

The authors describe the approach as simple to implement, requiring little hyperparameter tuning and providing stable training. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and 64-by-64 ImageNet show competitive performance, including cases where SMT or SMD surpass existing methods. The contribution is a common mixture-score formulation that accommodates both direct training and diffusion-model distillation for one-step generation.
icml-2025-score-of-mixture-training-one-.tldr: Score-of-Mixture Training learns one-step generators from real–generated mixture scores, supporting both training from scratch and diffusion-model distillation.

paragraphs: Speech decoding from brain activity has advanced through large datasets from individual participants. Combining recordings across people is harder because anatomy, experimental tasks, and recording hardware vary. This paper develops an architecture and neuroscience-informed self-supervised learning objectives designed to learn from those heterogeneous recordings.

The approach scales to nearly 400 hours of magnetoencephalography data from 900 subjects. Its reported generalization spans participants, datasets, and tasks, including subjects not previously seen by the model. Learning across these differences is the central objective: it makes recordings from multiple sources useful for a shared speech-decoding model.

The authors report improvements of 15–27% over state-of-the-art models and performance matching surgical decoding using non-invasive data in their evaluation. These findings support the potential of scaling speech decoding through shared training across heterogeneous brain datasets. The comparison concerns reported decoding performance; the broader contribution is a training approach that can draw on diverse recordings rather than depending solely on a large dataset for one individual.
icml-2025-the-brains-bitter-lesson-scali.tldr: Self-supervised learning across heterogeneous brain recordings improves speech decoding and generalizes to unseen subjects using nearly 400 hours of non-invasive MEG data.

paragraphs: Explaining a time-series prediction requires identifying both which points matter and whether they push the prediction upward or downward. The paper finds that conventional Integrated Gradients can capture both directions, but existing evaluation metrics can hide this ability by allowing opposing contributions to cancel.

The authors introduce Cumulative Prediction Difference and Cumulative Prediction Preservation to assess identification of significant positive and negative points. Under these metrics, conventional Integrated Gradients outperforms recent alternatives. This changes the assessment of existing methods by making the evaluation sensitive to an aspect of attribution that magnitude-focused comparisons can overlook.

The paper then addresses a separate weakness of applying Integrated Gradients directly to time series. Its generated paths can ignore temporal relationships and create out-of-distribution samples. TIMING adds temporal awareness while retaining the method's theoretical properties. Experiments on synthetic and real-world time-series benchmarks show improvements over existing explanation baselines. Together, the evaluation metrics and algorithm address both how explanations are judged and how they are constructed.
icml-2025-timing-temporality-aware-integ.tldr: TIMING makes Integrated Gradients sensitive to temporal structure, while new evaluation metrics preserve the distinction between positive and negative contributions.

paragraphs: Two embedding models can achieve similar classification performance while organizing the same samples differently. This paper proposes SPEC, a framework for making those differences interpretable by identifying groups of samples that cluster differently in the two representation spaces. The comparison uses a shared reference dataset.

SPEC constructs kernel matrices from the embeddings, capturing relationships between samples. It then analyzes the eigendecomposition of the difference between those matrices to find clustering structure that the models capture differently. The authors provide a scalable implementation whose computational complexity grows linearly with the number of samples, enabling comparisons on large datasets.

The framework also supports an optimization problem for aligning embeddings so that clusters represented by one model are captured by the other. Numerical results demonstrate both comparison and alignment on ImageNet and MS-COCO. The contribution goes beyond a single downstream score by locating disagreements in sample-group structure and using those same disagreements as targets for bringing representations into closer agreement.
icml-2025-towards-an-explainable-compari.tldr: SPEC identifies and aligns clustering differences between embeddings through spectral analysis of their kernel-matrix difference.

paragraphs: Three-dimensional vision-language learning has less large-scale training data available than its two-dimensional counterpart. UniVLG addresses this imbalance with a shared architecture initialized mostly from pretrained 2D models and trained on both 2D and 3D data. The aim is to transfer existing visual-language capabilities into settings with depth information.

A shared language-conditioned mask decoder grounds objects in both RGB and RGB-D images. The paper reports that this mask-based approach outperforms box-based alternatives. It also introduces 2D-to-3D lifting strategies to reduce the gap between modalities, allowing 2D training data to contribute to improved 3D performance.

UniVLG achieves state-of-the-art results across multiple evaluated 3D grounding tasks. Joint training improves performance across modalities without sacrificing 2D capabilities. The approach also removes dependence on reconstructed 3D meshes and ground-truth object proposals, supporting evaluation more closely aligned with embodied sensing. These findings show how shared components, transferred initialization, and cross-modal training can help compensate for limited 3D data.
icml-2025-unifying-2d-and-3d-vision-lang.tldr: UniVLG transfers pretrained 2D capabilities into a shared 2D–3D grounding architecture, improving evaluated 3D performance while preserving 2D capabilities.
